Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Vignette:
Mai Tran was thirty-five years old, a physical therapist at a suburban outpatient clinic, and she had been married for six years to a man named David. She had come to therapy because she could no longer endure the way her own skin felt like a trap. The trouble had begun eighteen months earlier, during an argument in their kitchen. David had been angry about a credit card bill, and when Mai had tried to walk away from the table, he had grabbed her by the upper arm, his fingers digging in hard enough to leave bruises, and forced her back into her chair. He had not let go until she had agreed to hand over her paycheck. That was the first time he had ever used physical force, though the emotional cruelty had been building for years. What Mai could not shake, what had begun to dismantle her life, was not just the memory of that moment but the way the memory returned as though it were happening right then. When it came, she felt the pressure of his grip on her arm, the strange heat of his palm against her skin, and the absolute certainty that she was trapped again. The temperature of that touch—warm, insistent, unyielding—had become a sensor that her body now scanned for constantly.

In the months that followed, Mai found herself unable to explain to anyone what had happened. Whenever she tried to tell a friend or a colleague, the words would scatter. She would start describing the kitchen, the bill, the way David’s voice had gone flat, and then she would lose the thread entirely, her throat tightening until she had to stop. She had come to believe that she could not tell the story because the story was too shameful, and that the shame was proof that something was fundamentally wrong with her. She was certain that the event had happened because of the way she had acted—she should have just given him the money immediately, she should not have argued, she should have known better. This conviction had settled into her bones: there was something defective in her, some weakness that had invited this treatment, and that defect was now visible to everyone who looked at her. She felt permanently humiliated, as though the bruise on her arm had been a brand.

Her work as a physical therapist became a daily minefield. Touch was the currency of her profession, and she had always been skilled at it—knowing exactly where to apply pressure, how to guide a patient’s limb through a range of motion. Now, every time her hands made contact with a patient’s skin, she felt a spike of alarm. The warmth of another person’s body, the sensation of flesh under her palm, sent her straight back to that kitchen. She began to dread certain patients—the ones who needed manual therapy, the ones who were large or male or who spoke in loud voices. She found herself avoiding those cases, delegating them to colleagues, and when she could not delegate, she would go through the motions mechanically, her mind half-dissociated, her hands trembling afterward. The consequence was that her caseload shrank, and her supervisor noticed. Mai had been up for a promotion to senior therapist; that conversation had quietly been shelved.

She spent her evenings dwelling on how she used to be before that night. Before David, before the kitchen, she had been confident, quick to laugh, someone who moved through the world without checking every exit. She mourned that woman with a grief that felt bottomless. And she spent even more time dwelling on how the event could have been prevented. If she had not bought that dress, if she had not taken that shift, if she had just said yes instead of no. The rumination was relentless, a loop she could not step out of, and it left her exhausted and hollow.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. A new patient, an elderly man recovering from a hip replacement, had reached out and lightly touched her forearm to get her attention. The touch was gentle, neutral, entirely appropriate. But the temperature of his hand—warm, exactly the warmth of David’s palm—had sent Mai into a full flashback in the middle of the treatment room. She had frozen, her vision tunneling, her heart slamming, and she had been unable to speak for nearly a minute. The patient had been confused and apologetic; Mai had excused herself and spent the rest of the shift hiding in the supply closet. That night, she had finally called a therapist. She was terrified that she was losing her career, her marriage, and herself. She was hoping, more than anything, that someone could help her stop feeling like the event was still happening, that she could find a way to live in her own body again without the constant, silent scream.
